messages.author: 82da943574067f5f
messages.subject: Pattern of missing data
parts:
Hi folks,
I have a dataset with around 100 individuals drawn from six populations. Around half of the individuals (all of the ones from two of the populations) have very high missing data for the DArT called SNPs (call rate < 40%). For the others, missing data is low to moderate (call rate > 60%). This doesn't appear to be due to poor DNA quality as the missing data is in a distinct pattern on a smearplot.

However, if most of the missing data is filtered out, results of PCA, pairwise Fst and other analyses among all individuals are roughly as expected based on their geographic separation.

For the presence/absence of a sequence tag data set there is generally only low missing data for all individuals (call rate > ~90%). A PCA plot generated after moderate standard filtering for this dataset is also pretty much as expected based on sampling locations.

Any ideas on what could be the cause of the pattern in the missing SNP data? I guess duplicated regions of the genome could be an explanation, but I'm not sure how likely that is on this scale - the pattern of missing data is quite stark.

messages.author: d87216285ace7535
messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Pattern of missing data
parts:
Sometimes I see datasets a little bit like that, but I usually find that
after filtering I still have plenty of loci. 2000-5000 loci is more
than enough for most standard phylogeographic type analyses.

How many loci do you have in the dart file, vs how many after filtering?

What sort of organisms are we talking about here?

I also find it helpful to consider different filtering strategies
depending on whether you want more individuals, or more loci as one
tries to reduce missing data. If you want more loci then get rid of
individuals with higher missing data first. I often find it useful to
work out which individuals have too much missing data and remove them
automatically when I first read the data file in (by having a column in
the metadata file with a unique value for individuals I want to
exclude). Often outgroup samples will have the most missing data, but
you may wish to keep them, but then at times ingroup samples will be
poor, but can't be removed by the filtering command gl.filter.callrate
without also removing the outgroups too.

Cheers
Peter Unmack

messages.author: f7c335e987e6a186
messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Pattern of missing data
parts:
Thanks Peter.

I have ~16K SNPs after filtering on secondaries. After omitting a couple of individuals that have very high missing data I can filter on call rate across loci with t = 0.9 and after other standard filters end up with ~1500 loci, which I think is just about enough. For the silico DArT presence/absence data I still have ~8K loci even after filtering. This is for a mammal species in this case. What concerns me is the possibility that the distinct pattern of missingness across loci for the SNP dataset represents something biologically significant that is different between the individuals that have high missing data dnd those that don't. If it was just poor DNA quality for some of the samples I'd expect the pattern of missingness to be random.

messages.author: 592079bda2cb3220
messages.subject: Re: Pattern of missing data
parts:
Hi,

Some of the reasons I can think of are:
- cryptic species
- chromosome re-arrangement

You could investigate other hypotheses if you have a reference genome or a reference genome from a close species. Then you could map your SNPs using the function gl.blast. 

It would also be a good idea to ask directly to DArT. 

Cheers,
Luis

messages.author: 9e12eec50c435b60
messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Pattern of missing data
parts:
Hi Peter,

You have some good suggestions there from others. I guess I would add that missing data has two sources. The first is that the SNP call for a particular individual at a particular locus fails because the read depth is not sufficient to ensure all target sections of the genome are detected. At full coverage the read depth is about 21x on average, at half coverage only 12x. The second reason for a missed call is that there is a mutation at one or both of the restriction enzyme sites. The SilocoDArT data is heavily filtered by DArT to validate the "missing" data to retain only evidence of absence.

Let's say it is missing data because of failure to detect (absence of evidence). So you can have a go at filtering your data on read depth, say with a threshold of 8x, and then reexamine the missing data profile for the SNP genotype data. If it improves, then you have an indication of what is going on. The difference between the SNP genotype data and the SNP SilicoDArT data is also an indication that you have an unacceptable admixture of absence of evidence and evidence of absence calls in the SNP genotype data. The idea would be to filter on read depth and perhaps more heavily on call rate to overcome this.

If they are real missing data, that is arising from mutations at the restriction enzyme site, you could get the pattern you describe for example if the mutations at the restriction enzymes site occurred in a recent ancestor of the populations with the poor call rate. Not much you can do about this as it is a feature of the biology of the taxon in its spatial context. The fact that there are so many of these missing values does suggest long term accumulation and perhaps cryptic species, but that would be a port of last call.

Of course there is the possibility of batch effects, and so turning to DArT to discuss the issue is a good suggestion from Luis. They will have a better foundational level of understanding the data, and may be able to shed light on it.

Hope this helps.  A
